Bench height and posture — wrists level,:
The one you cannot see yourself doing wrong, which is why it is first.

- BENCH HEIGHT: sit so your forearms run roughly PARALLEL TO THE FLOOR with fingers on the keys. Elbows level with, or a shade above, the white keys. Too low and you press with a bent wrist; too high and you lose weight.
- DISTANCE: far enough back that your elbows stay slightly in front of your torso, not pinned to your sides. Sit on the front half of the bench, not back against it.
- WRISTS LEVEL means the back of the hand continues the line of the forearm — no dip below the keys, no arch above. Rest a pencil across the back of your hand; it should not roll off.
- SHOULDERS DOWN and still. If they creep up, you are lifting instead of dropping.
- FEET FLAT on the floor, right foot near the sustain pedal even when unused.

Check it in a mirror or a phone video once a week for the first month. Bad posture becomes invisible in about three days.
Finger numbers 1-5, both hands, named wi:
1 is the THUMB, 2 index, 3 middle, 4 ring, 5 little — in both hands. So the two thumbs are both 1 and face each other.

Every book, every fingering mark and every teacher uses these. Not knowing them cold makes written fingering unreadable, and written fingering is most of what makes a passage playable.

Drill: say a number, play that finger on both hands without looking at your hands. Then have someone call them out. Two minutes a day until it is instant.
Find any C on the keyboard; name every w:
The black keys come in groups of TWO and THREE. C is the white key immediately LEFT of any group of two. That is the whole trick, and it is the only landmark you need.

From C, the white keys run C D E F G A B and repeat. One C to the next is an OCTAVE. Middle C is the C nearest the middle of an 88-key board, just left of the brand name on most pianos.

Drill: close your eyes, put a finger anywhere, open them, name the key. Then find every F on the instrument — F is immediately left of any group of three.
The black-key pattern of 2 and 3; sharps:
A black key is named by its neighbours. The black key right of C is C SHARP; the same key is also D FLAT, because it is left of D. One key, two names — they are ENHARMONIC, and which name is used depends on the key you are in.

Sharp means raised a semitone, flat means lowered a semitone. A SEMITONE is the distance to the very next key, black or white.

Note that E-F and B-C have no black key between them — they are a semitone apart already. That irregularity is why scales need fingering patterns rather than one rule.
Five-finger pattern C-G, right hand, eve:
Right hand: thumb on middle C, one finger per white key up to G under the 5th. Play C D E F G and back down, one finger each, no shifting.

EVENLY is the entire exercise and it is harder than it sounds. Listen for two faults:
- Volume: the 4th finger will be weaker and the thumb louder. Make them match.
- Timing: the gap between notes should not change. Count out loud, one number per note.

Play from the knuckle, letting the arm's weight through — not by pressing with the fingertip. Keep the hand quiet; only the playing finger moves.
Five-finger pattern C-G, left hand, even:
Left hand: 5th finger on the C below middle C, thumb on G. So the pattern runs the other way round — the little finger takes the lowest note.

The left hand is worse than the right at this and sounds it. Give it twice the time and do not let the right hand's standard set your expectations.

Same two faults to listen for, plus one more: the left hand tends to drop its wrist. Keep it level.
Legato — two notes joined with no gap an:
LEGATO is a connected line. The next key goes down at the exact moment the previous one comes up — so the two notes touch and never sound together.

The test is audible. Play C then D slowly:
- A GAP means you lifted early. The line breaks.
- An OVERLAP means you lifted late. It smudges.

Practise on two notes until it is clean, then three, then the five-finger pattern. This is the single most important touch on the instrument and the thing that makes playing sound like music rather than typing.
Staccato — short, from the wrist, not th:
STACCATO is detached: the key is released almost immediately, so each note is separated by silence.

The motion comes from the WRIST, a small bounce, with the forearm quiet. Playing staccato from the arm is slow, tiring, and uncontrollable at speed.

Alternate: four bars legato, four bars staccato, same five notes. The contrast teaches both better than either alone.
Treble staff: C-G on lines and spaces, n:
Five lines, four spaces. The treble clef curls around G — the second line from the bottom is G.

Middle C sits on a short line BELOW the staff. Then D in the space below the first line, E on the first line, F in the first space, G on the second line.

Do not learn mnemonics for all nine positions. Learn two LANDMARKS — middle C below the staff, and G on the second line — and count up or down from whichever is nearer. Reading by landmark is how fluent readers actually do it; reciting "Every Good Boy" is what keeps people slow forever.
Bass staff: C-G below middle C, named at:
The bass clef's two dots sit either side of the fourth line up: that line is F.

Middle C is on a short line ABOVE the bass staff — the mirror of its position below the treble staff. That is the one fact that connects the two clefs.

Landmarks here: middle C above the staff, and F on the fourth line. Count from those.

The bass staff feels alien for a few weeks because the same line means a different note than in treble. That passes, and only with volume.
The grand staff — middle C in both clefs:
Treble above, bass below, braced together. Middle C can be written below the treble staff OR above the bass staff — the SAME key, two notations.

It appears twice because the two staves overlap by a note. The gap between them is not a gap in pitch; it is where middle C lives.

Exercise: write middle C both ways, play it, and say out loud "same key". It sounds trivial and it removes the most common early confusion outright.
Note values: whole, half, quarter:
- WHOLE note: hollow, no stem. Four beats.
- HALF note: hollow with a stem. Two beats.
- QUARTER note: filled with a stem. One beat.

A beat is whatever you are counting, not a fixed length of time. At 60 bpm a beat is a second; at 120 it is half.

Drill: clap each while counting aloud "one two three four". Hold a whole note for all four counts — holding is as much a skill as striking, and beginners consistently cut long notes short.
4/4 and bar lines; counting aloud while:
The top number is how many beats in a bar; the bottom is which note gets one beat. 4/4 is four quarter-note beats per bar. Bar lines mark the groups.

COUNT OUT LOUD. Not in your head — out loud. It is the only way to catch a rhythm being guessed, because your voice cannot fudge a duration the way your fingers can.

This feels childish for about a week and then it stops, because by then you can hear when you are wrong.
3/4 and the feel of three against four:
Three beats a bar. The emphasis falls on 1, so it swings rather than marches: ONE two three, ONE two three.

Play the same five-finger pattern in 4/4 and then 3/4 and listen to how different it feels with no notes changed. Metre is not bookkeeping; it is where the weight goes.

Waltzes, minuets and a great deal of early repertoire are in 3/4, so this is not an aside.
Rests, counted as carefully as notes:
A rest is a measured silence, not a pause for breath. A quarter rest is exactly as long as a quarter note.

Beginners treat rests as optional and lose time in them, which destroys the metre. Count a rest ALOUD and keep the hand still on the key bed — do not lift dramatically.

Drill: a bar of quarter notes, then a bar of quarter rests, repeated, counting throughout. The silence should be as exact as the sound.
Eighth notes and subdividing the beat:
Two eighth notes fit one beat. Count them "one-and-two-and-three-and-four-and" — the "and" is the second half of the beat.

SUBDIVIDING is the thing to learn here, and it is the fix for most rhythm problems that are not reading problems. Once you can feel the half-beat, uneven playing becomes obvious rather than merely wrong.

Keep counting aloud, including the "ands".
Play a written four-bar melody, right ha:
The first real reading. Four bars, right hand only, in C.

Method, in this order:
1. Name every note aloud WITHOUT playing.
2. Clap the rhythm while counting aloud, without the keyboard.
3. Then play, slowly, still counting aloud.

Most mistakes are rhythm, not pitch, and separating the two finds them. Do not speed up to get to the end — slow and correct becomes fast later; fast and wrong becomes a habit.
Play a written four-bar melody, left han:
Same method, bass clef, left hand.

It will be noticeably harder, for two reasons: the clef is less familiar and the hand is weaker. Expect it to take two or three times as long, and do not conclude anything about your ability from that.
Sight-read: four new bars a day, one han:
The habit that starts here and never ends. Four bars you have never seen, one hand, every day.

Two rules, and they are the whole exercise:
- NEVER STOP. Play through the mistake and keep the beat. Stopping to fix things trains stopping.
- Choose material well BELOW what you can play. Sight-reading is fluency practice, not a challenge.

Four bars is nothing — a minute a day. Doing it for a year is the difference between a reader and someone who memorises pieces slowly. §It is the skill most self-taught players neglect until it is the thing stopping them.
Both hands in parallel motion, five-fing:
Both hands playing C D E F G at the same time — right hand up from middle C, left hand up from the C below. Same finger numbers at the same moment, which makes this the easiest hands-together case.

Listen for whether the hands are actually TOGETHER. They usually are not: one leads by a fraction. Record it on a phone if you cannot hear it — the recording is merciless and useful.
Both hands in contrary motion:
Hands moving in opposite directions: right hand up C D E F G while the left hand goes down from middle C.

Harder than parallel, because the same finger number no longer means the same direction, and genuinely useful — most scales hands-together start life as contrary motion because the fingering lines up symmetrically.

Slowly, together, counting aloud.
Left-hand single notes under a right-han:
The real texture of beginner repertoire: melody in the right hand, single sustained notes or simple intervals underneath.

The difficulty is INDEPENDENCE — the left hand holding while the right moves. Practise hands separately until each is automatic, then put them together at half the speed you think you need.

If it falls apart, the answer is almost always "slower", not "again".
A first piece, hands together, read from:
A real piece, read rather than copied by ear or from a video.

Work in this order, and the order matters: hands separately, then a few bars hands together, then join the sections. Learning a whole piece one hand at a time and then combining it at the end is harder than doing it four bars at a time.

Slowly enough to be correct. The tempo mark is a destination, not an instruction for today.
Dynamics: p, mf, f — produced by touch,:
- p (piano): soft
- mf (mezzo-forte): moderately loud
- f (forte): loud

They are RELATIVE, not absolute volumes, and they come from how fast the key goes down — which is weight and speed, not force. The pedal does not make things louder; it makes them blurrier.

Exercise: play the five-finger pattern at p, then mf, then f, with no change in tempo or evenness. Most beginners speed up as they get louder.
Phrasing: shape a four-bar phrase rather:
A phrase is a musical sentence. It has a shape: it goes somewhere and comes back.

In practice: a slight swell toward the phrase's high point or its third bar, and a slight relaxation at the end. Not much — a few percent of volume and a breath of time.

Eight notes played exactly equally is correct and dead. This is the difference between right notes and music, and it is where playing starts being worth listening to.
Play to a metronome at 60 without drifti:
60 bpm, one beat a second. Play the five-finger pattern and a simple piece against it.

You will drift, and the direction tells you something: speeding up means you are rushing the easy bars; slowing means the hard bars are not learned yet.

Do not practise everything to a metronome — it flattens phrasing. Use it to find where the time goes wrong, then fix that spot.
Sight-read: four new bars a day, hands t:
The daily habit, upgraded. Four unfamiliar bars, both hands, no stopping, well below your playing level.

Hands together roughly doubles the difficulty, so drop the material's difficulty to match. The rule is unchanged: keep the beat, play through the mistake.
FUN · Minecraft — Wet Hands (C418), righ:
The first piece anyone will recognise, and deliberately early because the classical path is long.

The right-hand melody is slow, in a comfortable range, and repeats — genuinely playable with stage 2's reading. Find a simplified arrangement on MuseScore and take only the top line for now.

The full version comes back at stage 3 when both hands are available.
FUN · Zelda — Zelda’s Lullaby, melody on:
Six notes, slow, and instantly recognisable. In 3/4, which makes it useful practice for the metre from stage 2.

Melody only here. It is one of the clearest examples of how little is needed for a tune to work — which is also a composition lesson.
FUN · Minecraft — Wet Hands, hands toget:
Now with the left hand: held chords underneath a simple melody, which is exactly the texture from "left-hand single notes under a right-hand melody".

Why this piece earns its place: the left hand is slow and sustained, so all the difficulty is coordination rather than notes. It sounds far more accomplished than it is to play.
FUN · My Neighbour Totoro — Path of the:
Hisaishi, and the gentlest introduction to his writing. Easy arrangements exist at roughly grade 1-2 on MuseScore.

Mostly stepwise melody over simple broken chords. Watch the pedal markings if the arrangement has them — you have not learned pedalling yet (stage 6), so play it without and add the pedal later.
FUN · Zelda — Song of Storms, easy arran:
In 3/4 and fast-feeling without being fast, which makes it a good test of whether the metre from stage 2 is solid.

The left hand is a repeating figure; the right carries the tune. Take the left hand alone until the pattern is automatic — then the piece is almost done.
C major, one octave, right hand, thumb p:
C D E F G A B C with fingering 1 2 3 1 2 3 4 5. The thumb passes UNDER the hand after E to take F.

The whole exercise is the thumb pass being inaudible. Two faults to listen for:
- A bump where the thumb lands — it is heavier than the other fingers and must be held back.
- A gap before the thumb — the hand is waiting rather than preparing. Move the thumb toward F WHILE 3 is still playing.

Coming down: 5 4 3 2 1 3 2 1, with 3 crossing OVER the thumb. Same rule, reversed.
C major, one octave, left hand:
Fingering 5 4 3 2 1 3 2 1 going up, 1 2 3 1 2 3 4 5 coming down — the mirror of the right hand.

The crossing happens in a different place, which is the only thing making this feel unfamiliar. Same two faults: no bump, no gap.
C major, two octaves, hands together, ev:
Both hands, two octaves, metronome at 60, one note per beat, then two notes per beat.

The hands cross their thumbs at DIFFERENT points, which is why hands-together scales are harder than either hand alone and why this takes longer than it looks like it should.

Evenly means no bumps anywhere — not at the thumb passes, not at the turn, not at the top.
G major and F major, one octave each han:
G major has one sharp (F#); F major has one flat (B♭).

G major fingers like C in the right hand (1 2 3 1 2 3 4 5). F major does NOT — the right hand uses 1 2 3 4 1 2 3 4, because the thumb must avoid the black key. That irregularity is the real lesson: fingering follows the black keys, not a rule.

Learn why each fingering is what it is, and the remaining ten scales largely explain themselves.
The circle of fifths; key signatures to:
Going up a fifth each time adds a sharp: C (none), G (1), D (2), A (3), E (4). Going down a fifth adds a flat: C, F (1), B♭ (2), E♭ (3), A♭ (4).

Sharps always appear in the order F C G D A E B. Flats in the reverse: B E A D G C F.

The practical use: a key signature with three sharps IS A major, and you know that without counting. Reading in an unfamiliar key stops being a note-by-note translation.
A natural minor, then harmonic, then mel:
A minor is C major's RELATIVE MINOR — same notes, different home note, so no key signature.

- NATURAL minor: A B C D E F G A. Just the white keys from A.
- HARMONIC minor: raise the 7th (G becomes G#). That gives the characteristic augmented-second step from F to G# and the sound everyone recognises as "minor".
- MELODIC minor: raise the 6th and 7th going up (F# and G#), and lower them again coming down. It differs ascending and descending, which is unusual and worth hearing.

Play all three back to back. The difference is more obvious in the ear than on the page.
Tonic triads and their inversions in C,:
A triad is three notes: root, third, fifth. C major is C E G.

- ROOT position: C E G
- FIRST inversion: E G C (third at the bottom)
- SECOND inversion: G C E (fifth at the bottom)

Same three notes, three shapes, three different weights. Inversions are what let a chord progression move without the hand leaping, which is most of what good left-hand writing does.

Play all three inversions of C, G and F, both hands, until the shapes are in the hand.
Broken chords and arpeggios: C, G, F:
A BROKEN CHORD plays the triad's notes one at a time within the hand's span. An ARPEGGIO carries it across octaves and needs a thumb pass, like a scale.

Right-hand C arpeggio: 1 2 3 1 2 3 5. The thumb pass is the same skill as the scale's and is harder because the leap is wider.

Keep the hand quiet and let the arm carry it along the keyboard. Reaching with the fingers produces a lurch at every pass.
All twelve major scales, two octaves, ha:
The tedious and non-negotiable one.

Suggested order: C, G, D, A, E (adding a sharp each time), then F, B♭, E♭, A♭, D♭, and finally B and G♭/F#.

What this buys you is not scale-playing. It is that the fingering patterns live in the hand, so reading a piece in five flats stops requiring you to work out every note — your fingers already know where that key lies. There is no shortcut and no substitute.
All twelve harmonic minor scales, two oc:
Same twelve keys, harmonic minor form — raised 7th, each time.

The augmented second between the 6th and raised 7th makes the fingering feel awkward in a way major never does. That awkwardness IS the scale; do not smooth it out.

Pair each with its relative major (A minor with C major, E minor with G major) so the key signatures reinforce rather than compete.
Sight-read: a piece in a key with three:
The daily reading, now in an unfamiliar key.

This is where the scale work pays off and where you find out whether it took. If reading in E major is still note-by-note translation, the scales are not in the hand yet.

Same rules: unfamiliar, below your level, no stopping.
FUN · Naruto — Sadness and Sorrow:
Slow, in a comfortable key, and famous. Beginner arrangements are everywhere.

Why it belongs at stage 4: it sits mostly within the hand with a simple broken-chord left hand, so it is a direct application of this stage's inversions and broken chords rather than a departure from them.
FUN · Undertale — Home:
Short, slow, mostly stepwise, with a repeating left-hand figure. One of the most playable pieces in any game soundtrack.

Good for phrasing, which stage 3 introduced and which this piece needs to not sound mechanical — it is simple enough that shaping is the only thing left to get right.
Bach — Minuet in G, BWV Anh. 114 (Anna M:
The conventional first real piece, and for good reason: two independent lines, neither hard alone, both in G major, and in 3/4 so the metre work applies.

What it demands that nothing before it did: the hands play DIFFERENT MUSIC rather than melody-and-accompaniment. Practise each hand to the point of being able to play it while reading the other.

Baroque, so play it with little or no pedal — the clarity between lines is the point.
Bach — Minuet in G minor, BWV Anh. 115:
The companion to the G major, and the first minor-key piece. The harmonic minor work from stage 4 is audible in it.

Slightly harder than its major pair, and often published alongside it. Learn both and play them back to back — in the Notebook they belong together.
Schumann — Melody, Op. 68 no. 1 (Album f:
From a collection written for children and not childish. Simple right-hand melody over a broken-chord left hand.

What it teaches is PHRASING, which Bach does not foreground. The melody has an obvious shape and sounds wrong played flat, so it forces the stage 3 lesson to become real.
FUN · Howl’s Moving Castle — Merry-Go-Ro:
The Hisaishi everyone wants to play. This is the EASY arrangement — grade 2-3 — not the concert version, which returns at stage 7.

In 3/4, waltz feel, and a direct application of everything in stage 5: a melody needing shape over a moving left hand.

Make sure the arrangement you download is the simplified one. The difficulty claim here is about the arrangement, not the piece.
FUN · Spirited Away — Always With Me (It:
Gentle, slow, and simpler than it sounds. Sits comfortably at stage 5.

Mostly a sustained melody over broken chords, which is the texture this whole stage is about.
FUN · Fullmetal Alchemist — Brothers:
Minor key, slow, and strongly phrased — a direct test of the Schumann lesson on a piece you actually want to play.

Arrangements vary widely in difficulty; take a simple one. The tune carries it.
Schumann — Soldier’s March, Op. 68 no. 2:
From the same collection. Rhythmically crisp where the Melody was lyrical, so it trains the other half of touch — staccato and dotted rhythms rather than legato line.

Short, and a useful contrast to play immediately after the Melody.
Burgmüller — Arabesque, Op. 100 no. 2:
The first piece that needs any speed, and the first that sounds hard to a listener.

Rapid right-hand figures over a simple left hand, in A minor. The difficulty is evenness at tempo, which is the scale work applied to a real piece rather than an exercise.

Start it at half tempo and do not raise the speed until it is clean. It is a famous trap for rushing.
Clementi — Sonatina Op. 36 no. 1, first:
The first piece with a FORM — sonata form in miniature: two themes, a development, a return.

Why it comes here: it is long enough to require practising in sections rather than from the top, which is a practice skill as much as a playing one. Learn the second theme first; everyone neglects it because it comes later.

Classical style, so clean articulation and almost no pedal.
Beethoven — Für Elise, main section:
The famous A section only. Everyone plays it and most play it badly, which makes it a good diagnostic.

The difficulty is the right hand's repeated turn figure staying even and light while the left hand's broken chords stay quiet underneath. It is a balance problem, not a notes problem.

The middle sections are harder and can wait.
Satie — Gymnopédie no. 1:
Slow, spacious, and the first piece where pedal genuinely matters — which is awkward, because pedalling is stage 6.

Play it without pedal first and hear what is missing. That is the most useful possible preparation for stage 6, because you will know exactly what the pedal is for before learning how to use it.

Technically the easiest piece in this stage and musically the hardest. It has nowhere to hide.
Sight-read: a complete short piece, firs:
An upgrade from four bars: a whole short piece, start to finish, first time through, at half tempo.

The point is CONTINUITY — holding the shape of a piece together while reading it, which four bars never tests. Still no stopping.
Hanon 1-5, hands together, 60bpm, evenly:
The first five Hanon exercises, hands together, metronome at 60.

Hanon is mechanical by design and that is its only virtue: finger independence and evenness with nothing musical to think about. Do not expect it to be interesting.

Two rules that make it worth the time rather than harmful:
- Stop the moment your hand aches. Hanon played tense builds tension.
- Listen for the 4th and 5th fingers being quieter and fix THAT, which is the entire point.
Hanon 1-10 at 80bpm:
Ten exercises, faster. The same two rules.

Raise the tempo only when the current one is clean — raising it to struggle is how injuries happen and how uneven playing gets learned at speed.
Czerny Op. 599, studies 1-10:
More musical than Hanon and more useful. Czerny wrote studies that sound like pieces and drill one specific difficulty each.

Work out what each study is FOR before practising it — scale passages, broken chords, a particular hand shape. A study practised without knowing its purpose is just a short piece.
Sustain pedal — syncopated pedalling, ch:
The pedal lifts the dampers so notes continue after the key is released. It is not a volume control and it is not a way to connect what your fingers cannot.

SYNCOPATED (or legato) pedalling is the technique that matters: the pedal comes UP and straight back DOWN just AFTER the new note sounds. Down-with-the-note blurs the change; this clears the old harmony and catches the new one.

Drill: play a slow chord progression and change the pedal after each chord. Listen for whether the previous chord is still audible — if it is, the lift was late.

Then go back to the Gymnopédie.
Scales at 100bpm, four octaves, hands to:
What stage 4's scales were building toward. Four octaves means two thumb passes each way per hand, at speed.

100 bpm with two notes per beat is 200 notes a minute. Evenness at that speed is only possible if the fingering is automatic, which is the test.
Chromatic scale, two octaves, both hands:
Every semitone, white and black. Standard fingering: 3 on the black keys, thumb and 2 alternating on the whites, with 1 2 on the two white-white pairs (E-F and B-C).

Useful out of proportion to its difficulty, because chromatic runs appear constantly in Romantic repertoire and the fingering never changes.
Octave reaches and the stretch between 1:
Playing C and the C above together, thumb and 5th finger.

Open the hand from the KNUCKLES, not by forcing the thumb and little finger apart at the tips. If it hurts, stop — hand size varies and forcing a stretch causes injury that takes months off.

Practise octaves as a relaxed drop, not a grip. Beethoven and Chopin both assume them.
Trills, mordents and the ornaments Bach:
Baroque scores are notated sparsely and assume the player knows the conventions.

- TRILL (tr): rapid alternation with the note above. In Baroque practice it usually starts ON THE UPPER note, not the written one — which is the part everybody gets wrong.
- MORDENT: a quick drop to the note below and back.
- APPOGGIATURA: a grace note leaning into the main note.

Learn these before returning to Bach at stage 7, where the Inventions and Preludes are full of them and the editions disagree with each other.
FUN · Death Note — L’s Theme:
Fast, driving, repetitive — and squarely a technique piece, which is why it sits in this stage rather than earlier.

It needs the evenness at speed that Hanon and Czerny are for, and it is a far better reason to have done them than they are on their own.
FUN · Final Fantasy X — To Zanarkand:
Slow and famous, with the broken-chord left hand that pedalling exists for. Play it immediately after the pedalling lesson.

Musically simple, so all the work is in balance and pedal — which is exactly this stage's content on a piece worth playing.
FUN · Undertale — Megalovania:
The speed test, and genuinely hard. It belongs here and not earlier.

Driving left-hand octaves under a fast right hand: it needs the octave work and the evenness from this stage. Take it in short sections at half tempo and expect it to take weeks.

Arrangements vary enormously; some are harder than the Chopin at stage 7.
Sight-read: a piece with pedal markings,:
The daily reading, now including the pedal.

Reading pedal markings while reading notes is a genuinely separate skill and most people simply ignore them. Observe them exactly, even where it sounds worse than your instinct — the instinct improves once the markings have been obeyed for a while.
Bach — Prelude in C, WTC Book I:
Unbroken broken chords, both hands, for the whole piece — the same figure moving through a harmonic sequence.

The difficulty is evenness over a long span and hearing the HARMONY rather than the pattern. Name the chord in each bar as you play it; the piece becomes music instead of an exercise the moment you can.

Almost no pedal. Bach's clarity is the whole effect.
Bach — Invention no. 1 in C, BWV 772:
Two genuinely equal voices, each carrying the subject in turn. The real introduction to counterpoint.

Practise each hand ALONE to performance standard — not merely playable — before combining. Then practise singing one line while playing the other. If you cannot hear both voices separately while playing, the audience cannot either.

This is the piece that teaches what Bach is actually doing.
Chopin — Prelude Op. 28 no. 4 in E minor:
A slow right-hand melody over relentless repeated left-hand chords.

Two difficulties, both new: keeping the left hand quiet and absolutely even for the whole piece without tensing, and shaping a melody that descends almost continuously without it sagging.

The first Chopin here because it is slow. It is not easy.
Chopin — Nocturne Op. 9 no. 2:
The famous one. Melody with ornamentation over a wide-spanning left hand, and the first piece requiring real RUBATO — flexible time in service of the line.

The left hand reaches well beyond an octave, so the octave work from stage 6 is a prerequisite rather than a nicety. Pedal is continuous and must be changed cleanly on every bass note.

It will take months. It is worth them.
Beethoven — Sonata Op. 49 no. 2, first m:
The accessible Beethoven sonata movement, and a real one — sonata form at full length rather than Clementi's miniature.

What it needs that nothing earlier did: structural thinking. Learn the exposition's two themes, the development, and the recapitulation as separate pieces of material, then assemble them. Practising from the top down is how a long movement stays unlearned for months.
Debussy — Clair de Lune:
Technically within reach by this stage and interpretively the hardest thing in the curriculum.

It needs pedal control, voicing within chords, extremely quiet playing that still speaks, and a sense of time that is nearly free. There are no mechanical difficulties to hide behind.

Save it for last in this stage.
Bach — a fugue from WTC Book I, voices a:
Three or four independent voices, with the subject passing between them.

The standard is stated in the milestone: the voices must be audible SEPARATELY. That means voicing — bringing one line forward in a texture where all the notes are played by the same two hands.

Pick a three-voice fugue first. C minor (BWV 847) is the usual recommendation. Practise voice by voice, then in pairs, before all three.
FUN · Howl’s Moving Castle — Merry-Go-Ro:
The concert arrangement, not the simplified one from stage 5 — which is why the same piece appears twice and why "difficulty is a claim about an arrangement" is in the document.

Having played the easy version two stages ago makes this far less daunting: the shape is known and only the execution is new.
FUN · Your Name — Nandemonaiya (RADWIMPS:
Modern, popular, and harder than it sounds — the rhythms are not square and the harmony moves more than a pop song's usually does.

Good at this stage because rubato and rhythmic flexibility are exactly what stages 6 and 7 built.
FUN · Attack on Titan — Vogel im Käfig:
Slow, sparse, and almost entirely about atmosphere. It needs the quiet control that Clair de Lune demands, on a much shorter piece.

A good preparation for the Debussy, in fact. Play it first.
FUN · Demon Slayer — Gurenge:
Fast, driving, and a straightforward speed and stamina test.

The least interesting of the fun pieces musically and the most satisfying to land. Expect the tempo to be the whole difficulty.
Sight-read: a movement you have never he:
The hardest form of the daily habit: a whole movement, both hands, never heard before, no recording consulted first.

Hearing it in your head FROM THE PAGE is the skill, and it is the one that separates a reader from a player who can read. Still no stopping.
Sight-read one new piece a week, below c:
Ongoing and permanent. One new piece a week, well below what you can play, read through without stopping.

Below your level is the instruction that gets ignored and the one that matters. Sight-reading improves with volume of easy material, not with difficulty.
Identify every interval within an octave:
Minor 2nd through to the octave, named by ear in any register.

Method: anchor each to a tune you know. Minor 2nd is the Jaws theme; major 3rd is the start of a major chord; perfect 5th is the Star Wars theme; octave is Somewhere Over the Rainbow. Anchors are not cheating — they are how everyone does it until it becomes direct.

Five minutes a day. It is the foundation of playing by ear and of transposing.
Tell major from minor from diminished by:
Three triad qualities, recognised regardless of which note is on the bottom.

Major is bright, minor is dark, diminished is unstable and wants to move. Inversions change the colour without changing the quality, which is what makes this harder than it sounds.

Play them with your eyes closed, in random inversions, and name them before looking.
Transpose a simple piece into three othe:
Take something you can play and play it in three other keys — by thinking in intervals and scale degrees rather than by reading transposed notation.

This is where the twelve scales from stage 4 stop being a chore. Transposing is only possible when the key's shape is in the hand, and it is the clearest proof that the scale work took.
Play a song from a lead sheet, left hand:
A lead sheet gives you the melody and chord symbols and nothing else. The left hand is yours to invent.

Start with root-position triads, then inversions for smoother movement, then broken patterns. The inversions from stage 4 are the whole toolkit.

This is the one place the classical path opens onto playing by ear, and it is worth having.
Memorise one piece completely, hands sep:
A whole piece from memory — and the test is being able to play each hand ALONE from memory, which almost nobody can do with a piece they think they have memorised.

Hands-together memory is mostly muscle memory, and it fails under pressure because it has no redundancy. Separate-hands memory is actual knowledge of the piece.

Pick something from stage 5 rather than stage 7.
Record yourself monthly and listen back:
Once a month, record a full piece and listen to all of it without stopping.

It is unpleasant and irreplaceable. You cannot hear your own playing while playing it — attention is on the hands — and the recording exposes the things you have stopped noticing: a rushed bar, a weak 4th finger, a pedal held too long.

Keep them. A year of monthly recordings is the clearest evidence of progress you will ever have.
FUN · Learn one song you actually want t:
The most important line in this curriculum.

One piece a month chosen for no reason except wanting to play it. Not graded, not sequenced, not justified.

The classical path is years long and the only people who finish it are the ones who kept playing things they loved while doing it.
